source.title: Measuring Monosemanticity in Sparse Autoencoders via Latent Activation Coherence

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures monosemanticity-related properties of sparse-autoencoder latents in vision and vision-language models. It does not measure the share or interpretability of the base models' own neurons, test explanation predictions on held-out activations, or assess the other specified claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's measurements concern SAE latents, not the base models' neurons or neuron poles. Its reported concept-deletion correlations are included as related SAE-feature findings under versions ["none"]. Figure-only TMS barplots and training trajectories are not extracted as rows because they do not test a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study proposes and validates a label-free monosemanticity metric (TMS) for sparse-autoencoder latents trained on DINOv3, CLIP and BLIP2 features. It never measures the share of interpretable neurons (or neuron poles) in a base model, never examines InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neurons, never builds attribution graphs, and never scores explanations against held-out activations. Its only mention of base-model neurons is a background statement that neurons can be polysemantic. None of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that TMS, a label- and encoder-free activation-coherence score for binarized SAE latents, is less affected by encoder anisotropy than embedding-based MS. They find it correlates with MS and with within-set variance, reveals differing SAE training dynamics, and is more strongly associated with deletion effectiveness under high anisotropy while competitive otherwise.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates a newly proposed, binarized-activation coherence metric on vision and vision-language sparse-autoencoder latents. It does not audit base-model neuron poles or test explanations on held-out neuron activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Results are reported across DINOv3, CLIP, and BLIP2; TopK and BatchTopK SAE regimes; K values 10, 32, and 64; and expansion factors ×2, ×4, and ×8. The paper also reports effects of encoder anisotropy and deletion-feature count N.

fits_no_version.finding: Across SAE configurations, SAE-level mean TMS and mean MS correlate positively with target-class accuracy drop after probe-ranked feature deletion. Correlations are mostly 0.6–0.92; for CLIP they are non-significant at N=16 and N=32 (TMS 0.406 and 0.158; MS 0.257 and −0.001).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For vision and vision-language SAEs, model-level monosemanticity scores are associated with feature-deletion effectiveness, and the strength of this association depends on encoder anisotropy and the number of deleted features.

fits_no_version.finding: Embedding-based MS rises with encoder anisotropy: CLIP scores highest, BLIP2 intermediate, DINOv3 lowest (Fig. 1). Per-neuron TMS–MS correlations are weaker for CLIP, down to 0.22 (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Embedding-similarity monosemanticity scores for SAE latents are inflated by encoder anisotropy, so this choice of scoring tool changes the apparent monosemanticity.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says the code is in an anonymous Zenodo repository with a private review link, to be made public on acceptance)
record.peer_reviewed: Accepted for post-workshop proceedings of the 8th International Workshop on eXplainable Knowledge Discovery in Data Mining (XKDD 2026); the provided paper is a preprint.
record.problems: The experiments use Mini-ImageNet and vision or vision-language models, not language-model neuron poles. The authors describe TMS as a proxy for activation-set coherence rather than ground-truth semantics; deletion associations are correlations, and the paper notes weaker probe accuracy for some CLIP settings. The code was not publicly available in the stated version.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's per-configuration TMS–MS and TMS–variance correlations (Tables 1 and 2), raw TMS/MS barplots (Figures 2–3), training trajectories (Figures 5–6), and deletion curves (Figure 7) were not extracted because they concern SAE-latent metrics and do not test a listed claim version. The table of anisotropy statistics was also omitted for the same reason.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares (about 90% one job, 7% two related jobs, 2–4% not understood); the study uses no language model neurons.
Neuron-level interpretability shares across dense and MoE language models and scale; only SAE latents on three vision/VLM encoders are scored.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose features, recursive generalization versus superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization and tools determine the share of interpretable base-model neurons. SAE K and expansion factor change SAE TMS, but that concerns SAE latents, not base neurons.
Neuron-based attribution graphs without a replacement model.
Whether explanations drawn from activating examples predict firing elsewhere. TMS and MS are activation-set coherence scores, not explanation-prediction tests.
Simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to no version and marked cannot_determine; all 36 rows match the values in Table 3. The subject is SAE latents, not base-model neurons, so this concerns a related but different construct. The anisotropy finding is loosely related to V4's point about tool dependence, but it concerns SAE features, so it is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares and the proportions of one-job, two-related-job, and not-understood poles.
Neuron-pole shares across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, or parameter scales up to trillions.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, recursive generalization, and superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tools determine the share of interpretable base-model neurons, including the stated InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons explain behavior without a replacement model.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict a neuron's firing on separate examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: It does not test or use the claim or cite its sources. It only treats neuron polysemanticity as background motivation for SAEs, so 'discusses' is the closest fit.

tranche.reason: Proposes the TMS metric for SAE latents and validates it. It never measures the share of interpretable base-model neurons or poles, and tests none of V1-V7.

source_check.notes: All 20 sampled Table 3 values and p-values match the text, in the right TMS/MS column, model and N. The states are cannot_determine because these are correlations between SAE-level metrics and deletion outcomes. The text has no base-model neuron interpretability measure; raw features appear only as a probe-accuracy baseline (Table B.1). The CLIP TMS value at N=16 (0.406, p=0.095) is also non-significant.
